Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, it appears that consuming alcohol in moderation, particularly when paired with meals, may have an inverse relationship with the risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). In other words, drinking alcohol with meals might lower the risk of AMI compared to not drinking at all. This is supported by two study findings:

1. A study found that alcohol drinking during meals was inversely related to the risk of acute MI.
2. Another study discovered that cue-induced behavioural activation, a specific model for understanding why people crave or are drawn to substances like alcohol, is more robust when consumed with food, suggesting that this aspect of craving might be sensitive to meal timing.

While there are other aspects to consider when it comes to the relationship between alcohol consumption and AMI, these two findings collectively suggest that incorporating alcohol into meals may have a protective effect on heart health in certain circumstances.
